questions.question: Which property of the plasma membrane lets it act as a useful selective barrier:
questions.explanation: A selectively permeable plasma membrane regulates which solutes enter and leave.

questions.question: Passive transport moves substances without:
questions.explanation: Passive transport proceeds spontaneously down a gradient without direct ATP expenditure.

questions.question: Which transport mechanism moves a solute AGAINST its gradient using ATP directly:
questions.explanation: Primary active transport uses direct energy from ATP or a primary energy source.

questions.question: Which transport process couples uphill solute movement to the downhill gradient of another ion:
questions.explanation: Secondary active transport harvests energy stored in an existing ion gradient.

questions.question: Small lipid-soluble gases like O2 and CO2 cross the bilayer mainly by:
questions.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules dissolve across the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion.

questions.question: Which factor contributes directly to the chemical component of an electrochemical gradient:
questions.explanation: Only concentration and electrical charge differences form an electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: Ungated membrane channels remain closed at all times and never permit solute passage.
questions.explanation: Ungated channels can remain open, whereas gated channels change their open state in response to stimuli.

questions.question: Movement of an ion through an open channel protein down its electrochemical gradient is passive.
questions.explanation: Channel-mediated movement following the electrochemical gradient requires no direct ATP.

questions.question: Facilitated diffusion relies on which membrane component to bind and release solutes:
questions.explanation: Carrier proteins bind the solute, change conformation, and release it across the membrane.

questions.question: Which nutrient commonly uses facilitated diffusion carrier pathways in appropriate tissues:
questions.explanation: Glucose and some amino acids use carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion down their gradients.

questions.question: Because carrier proteins have finite binding sites and turnover speed, facilitated diffusion shows:
questions.explanation: Limited carrier availability causes saturation kinetics at high concentrations.

questions.question: Which factor generally INCREASES the rate of diffusion across a membrane:
questions.explanation: A steeper driving gradient accelerates passive diffusion.

questions.question: Which factor generally SLOWS diffusion across a biological barrier:
questions.explanation: Thicker membranes or longer diffusion paths decrease diffusion rate.

questions.question: Which process moves fluid and dissolved solutes together due to a pressure gradient:
questions.explanation: Bulk flow carries fluid mass down a hydrostatic pressure gradient.

questions.question: Water and dissolved solutes pushed across capillary walls or renal glomeruli illustrate:
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure drives filtration across vascular and glomerular barriers.

questions.question: Net movement of water INTO a cell across a selective membrane is called:
questions.explanation: Water entering a cell down its osmotic gradient is endosmosis, not exosmosis, exocytosis, or pinocytosis.

questions.question: When diffusion distance across a membrane becomes much thicker, passive diffusion rate:
questions.explanation: Longer transport distance or thicker membranes slow diffusion.

questions.question: Osmotic pressure is defined as the pressure needed to:
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure opposes and halts net osmotic water flow across a selective membrane.

questions.question: The osmotic effect exerted specifically by plasma proteins is called:
questions.explanation: Colloid osmotic pressure due to blood plasma proteins is termed oncotic pressure.

questions.question: According to the chapter, typical human plasma oncotic pressure is approximately:
questions.explanation: The reference value cited for plasma oncotic pressure is roughly 25 mmHg.

questions.question: A transporter that moves ONE solute in ONE direction across the membrane is a:
questions.explanation: Uniport transports a single solute species unidirectionally.

questions.question: A transporter carrying TWO different solutes in the SAME direction is a:
questions.explanation: Symport (co-transport) moves two different solutes simultaneously in the same direction.

questions.question: An antiporter exchanges two solutes in:
questions.explanation: Antiport (counter-transport) couples movement of two solutes in opposite directions.

questions.question: During one complete cycle, the Na+/K+-ATPase pumps:
questions.explanation: Each cycle transfers three sodium ions outward and two potassium ions inward.

questions.question: Secondary active transport directly hydrolyzes ATP on the same transporter that moves glucose uphill.
questions.explanation: Primary active transport uses ATP directly; secondary active transport uses an existing downhill gradient.

questions.question: Because Na+/K+-ATPase moves one extra positive charge outward per cycle, it affects resting membrane electrical properties.
questions.explanation: Moving 3 Na+ out vs 2 K+ in creates a net outward positive charge transfer.

questions.question: Compared with intracellular fluid (ICF), extracellular fluid (ECF) is naturally:
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+ pump helps keep ECF sodium-rich and ICF potassium-rich.

questions.question: Calcium ATPases lower cytosolic Ca2+ concentration by:
questions.explanation: ATP-dependent Ca2+ pumps actively extrude or sequester calcium out of the cytosol.

questions.question: Hydrogen-ion pumps transfer which particle in tissues needing acid transport:
questions.explanation: H+-ATPases move protons across membranes in acid-secreting tissues.

questions.question: Which list gives substances associated with active transport in the chapter:
questions.explanation: The source highlights Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- among actively transported ions.

questions.question: Sodium-linked glucose transport is classified as:
questions.explanation: The Na+/glucose symporter uses the Na+ gradient created by Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.question: In Na+/H+ exchange across a membrane, the transport pattern is:
questions.explanation: Na+ and H+ travel in opposite directions, defining counter-transport / antiport.

questions.question: A sodium-glucose symporter is itself a primary ATP-hydrolyzing pump.
questions.explanation: The chapter flags this as a common exam trap: it taps into the secondary Na+ gradient rather than hydrolyzing ATP directly.

questions.question: Vesicular transport is used when macromolecules or particles are too large for channels or ordinary carriers.
questions.explanation: Cells enclose large cargo in membrane-bounded vesicles for endocytosis, exocytosis, or transcytosis.

questions.question: Which vesicular process takes up small portions of extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes:
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis invaginates the membrane to capture droplets of extracellular fluid.

questions.question: Specialized defense cells like neutrophils and macrophages perform phagocytosis to engulf:
questions.explanation: Phagocytes extend projections around large debris or microbes to enclose them.

questions.question: A large engulfed particle inside a phagocytic cell becomes enclosed within a membrane sac called a:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis encloses cargo inside a phagosome that fuses with lysosomes.

questions.question: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, uptake begins selectively when a ligand binds a:
questions.explanation: Ligand binding to a specific surface receptor initiates coated-pit clustering.

questions.question: What role does CLATHRIN play in receptor-mediated endocytosis:

options.A: It is the primary hormone receptor
options.B: It breaks down ATP to pump Na+
options.D: It is a membrane coating protein

questions.explanation: Clathrin coats the invaginating pit; it is a coat protein rather than the ligand receptor.

questions.question: Release of cellular secretory products when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane is:
questions.explanation: Exocytosis exports vesicular cargo into the extracellular space.

questions.question: Moving cargo across an endothelial cell by endocytosis on one face and exocytosis on the other is:
questions.explanation: Transcytosis ferries cargo from one pole of a cell to the opposite pole.

questions.question: After phagocytosis encloses a bacterium in a phagosome, digestive enzymes come from fusion with:
questions.explanation: Fusion with lysosomal compartments supplies hydrolytic enzymes to digest the cargo.

questions.question: Endocytosis always moves cargo out of the cell, whereas exocytosis brings extracellular fluid in.
questions.explanation: Endocytosis mediates entry into the cell; exocytosis mediates exit from the cell.

questions.question: Receptor-mediated endocytosis is more selective than ordinary fluid-phase pinocytosis.
questions.explanation: Receptor-ligand specificity selectively concentrates target molecules before vesicle formation.

questions.question: Why do cells require specialized membrane transport mechanisms:

options.B: To convert passive flow into DNA
options.D: To obtain O2/nutrients and remove wastes across a selective barrier

questions.explanation: Transport pathways move essential solutes and water across the selectively permeable bilayer.

questions.question: Which statement defines PASSIVE transport:

options.B: Spontaneous movement down a gradient without direct ATP
options.D: Movement of proteins against hydrostatic force

questions.explanation: Passive processes follow chemical or electrochemical gradients with no direct ATP consumption.

questions.question: Passive movement of an uncharged solute depends mainly on its:
questions.explanation: Electrical forces do not act directly on uncharged molecules; concentration drives them.

questions.question: Gated membrane channels open or close in response to:
questions.explanation: Channel gates respond to voltage changes or ligand binding.

questions.question: Which pair of molecules crosses the phospholipid bilayer easily by simple diffusion:
questions.explanation: Small lipid-soluble gases diffuse readily through the hydrophobic core.

questions.question: Water and charged ions rely heavily on membrane proteins rather than just lipids because:
questions.explanation: Channels supply water-filled transmembrane pores for hydrophilic particles.

questions.question: During facilitated diffusion, a carrier binds its solute and then:

options.A: Changes shape to release it across
options.B: Hydrolyzes ATP to force it uphill

questions.explanation: Conformational shape change shifts exposure of the binding site across the membrane.

questions.question: What limits the maximal rate of facilitated diffusion compared with simple lipid diffusion:

options.C: Finite number of carrier binding sites

questions.explanation: Carriers can become saturated when all binding sites are busy.

questions.question: If membrane thickness INCREASES, passive diffusion rate generally:
questions.explanation: Longer diffusion distance slows passive solute movement.

questions.question: Higher temperature generally affects diffusion rate by:
questions.explanation: Higher thermal motion increases diffusion rates.

questions.question: Fluid movement out of capillaries and into renal glomeruli driven by hydrostatic pressure is:
questions.explanation: Filtration is hydrostatic pressure-driven bulk movement through a barrier.

questions.question: In osmosis, water moves across a selective membrane toward the compartment with:
questions.explanation: Water diffuses net toward the higher effective concentration of water-attracting solutes.

questions.question: Water exiting a cell by osmosis is specifically termed:
questions.explanation: Outward osmotic water movement from a cell is exosmosis.

questions.question: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure is mainly generated by:
questions.explanation: Colloidal plasma proteins establish oncotic pressure (~25 mmHg).

questions.question: A membrane transporter moving TWO solutes in opposite directions performs:
questions.explanation: Antiporters mediate counter-transport in opposite directions.

questions.question: Moving glucose across a cell membrane by a single-solute carrier down its gradient uses:
questions.explanation: A uniporter moves one type of solute in one direction.

questions.question: How many potassium ions enter the cell per Na+/K+-ATPase cycle:
questions.explanation: The pump exchanges 3 Na+ outward for 2 K+ inward.

questions.question: Which energy source directly powers PRIMARY active transport:
questions.explanation: Primary active pumps couple solute movement directly to ATP hydrolysis.

questions.question: Because Na+/K+-ATPase runs continuously, cytosol stays relatively rich in:
questions.explanation: Active pumping keeps intracellular K+ high and intracellular Na+ low.

questions.question: In sodium-linked amino acid uptake across a membrane, both Na+ and the amino acid move:
questions.explanation: Na+-coupled amino acid transport is a classic symport (co-transport) pathway.

questions.question: Na+/Ca2+ exchange belongs to which transport category:
questions.explanation: Sodium downhill influx drives calcium uphill efflux in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which ion pump helps keep cytosolic Ca2+ concentration very low:
questions.explanation: Primary Ca2+-ATPases pump calcium out of the cytosol across membranes.

questions.question: What drives SECONDARY active transport at the carrier itself:

options.A: Direct ATP breakdown by that symporter
options.D: An ion gradient previously built by primary pumps

questions.explanation: Stored energy in the Na+ gradient powers uphill co- or counter-transport.

questions.question: Which term covers ALL membrane-vesicle routes carrying cargo across cells:
questions.explanation: Endocytosis, exocytosis, and transcytosis make up vesicular transport.

questions.question: Pinocytosis differs from phagocytosis primarily because pinocytosis takes up:
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis mediates fluid-phase uptake, whereas phagocytosis engulfs large particles.

questions.question: Neutrophils and macrophages use phagocytosis especially to clear:
questions.explanation: Immune phagocytes engulf pathogens and cell debris into phagosomes.

questions.question: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, selective specificity comes from:
questions.explanation: Specific surface receptors select target ligands before coated-pit invagination.

questions.question: Which protein forms the coat around invaginating vesicles in receptor-mediated endocytosis:
questions.explanation: Clathrin coats the membrane pit during selective endocytosis.

questions.question: Passage of cargo across an endothelial cell from lumen to tissue by vesicle uptake then release is:
questions.explanation: Transcytosis combines endocytosis on one side with exocytosis on the opposite side.

questions.question: One-minute review summary: passive transport ALWAYS moves:
questions.explanation: Passive diffusion and channels always follow a driving gradient.

questions.question: Which process does NOT require direct ATP or a stored ion gradient:
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive carrier-mediated movement down a gradient.

questions.question: During simple diffusion, which property makes a molecule pass SLOWER through lipids:
questions.explanation: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than small ones.

questions.question: Opposing electrical forces act as a barrier that slows diffusion of:
questions.explanation: Electrical gradients influence charged ions alongside concentration gradients.

questions.question: In the chapter memory table, bulk flow responds primarily to a:
questions.explanation: Bulk flow moves fluid masses down hydrostatic pressure differences.

questions.question: Oncotic pressure of roughly 25 mmHg helps hold water inside:
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins generate ~25 mmHg oncotic pressure inside capillaries.

questions.question: What distinguishes CO-TRANSPORT from COUNTER-TRANSPORT by direction:

options.C: Hydrostatic bulk flow vs passive osmosis

questions.explanation: Symporters execute co-transport in the same direction, whereas antiporters exchange solutes in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which transport term applies when ONE ion travels downhill to pull another ion the OPPOSITE way:
questions.explanation: Antiporters exchange two solutes in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which pair represents TWO secondary active transport examples from the chapter:
questions.explanation: Both rely on the Na+ gradient rather than direct ATP hydrolysis at that carrier.

questions.question: Which cell organelle fuses with a phagosome to supply digestive enzymes:
questions.explanation: Phagolysosomal fusion delivers hydrolytic enzymes for particle digestion.

questions.question: Releasing digestive enzymes or hormones from secretory vesicles to the outside occurs by:
questions.explanation: Exocytosis fuses secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane to expel contents.

questions.question: Both simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion move solutes down their gradients without ATP.
questions.explanation: Both are passive transport mechanisms driven by concentration or electrochemical gradients.

questions.question: Osmosis requires a primary ATPase pump for every water molecule that crosses the membrane.
questions.explanation: Osmosis is passive net movement of water across a selectively permeable barrier.

questions.question: Colloid osmotic pressure of plasma is approximately 250 mmHg.
questions.explanation: Typical plasma oncotic pressure is approximately 25 mmHg, not 250 mmHg.

questions.question: Uniporters carry two different solutes simultaneously in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: A uniporter moves one kind of solute; an antiporter moves two solutes in opposite directions.

questions.question: The Na+/K+-ATPase transfers 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per transport cycle.
questions.explanation: That 3:2 stoichiometry maintains low cytosolic Na+ and high cytosolic K+.

questions.question: Secondary active transport depends ultimately on gradients created by energy-dependent pumps elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Stopping Na+/K+-ATPase dissipates the Na+ gradient that powers secondary transport.

questions.question: Clathrin acts as the ligand-binding hormone receptor during receptor-mediated endocytosis.
questions.explanation: Clathrin is the coating protein lining the pit; specific surface receptors bind the ligand.

questions.question: Pinocytosis can bring dissolved extracellular solutes into the cell inside small vesicles.
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis invaginates the membrane around droplets of extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes.

questions.question: Transcytosis uses endocytosis on one side of a cell and exocytosis on the opposite side.
questions.explanation: Transcytosis transports cargo completely across barrier cells such as endothelium.

questions.question: Filtration moves water only from low hydrostatic pressure toward high hydrostatic pressure.
questions.explanation: Filtration drives fluid from higher hydrostatic pressure toward lower hydrostatic pressure.

questions.question: Why must cells balance selective permeability with active and passive transport pathways:

options.A: To allow unlimited free leakage of proteins
options.B: To exchange nutrients, water, and wastes selectively
options.C: To abolish all electrochemical gradients rapidly
options.D: To block oxygen entry into cytosol

questions.explanation: A barrier alone would starve cells unless regulated transport pathways cross it.

questions.question: Which distinction cleanly separates PRIMARY from SECONDARY active transport in the opening table:

options.A: Primary requires zero energy; secondary consumes clathrin
options.B: Primary moves only water; secondary moves only gases
options.C: Primary runs only downhill; secondary runs only in vesicles
options.D: Primary uses ATP directly at the pump; secondary taps an existing ion gradient

questions.explanation: Both move cargo uphill, but their immediate energy coupling differs.

questions.question: What determines the total driving force on potassium ions across a resting plasma membrane:

options.B: Both chemical concentration difference and electrical potential difference

questions.explanation: Charged ions respond to the combined electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: Unlike an uncharged solute, an ion moving passively responds to:
questions.explanation: Both concentration and voltage gradients act on charged ions.

questions.question: How does an UNGATED channel differ operationally from a GATED channel:

options.A: Ungated can remain open continuously; gated opens or closes upon stimulation
options.B: Ungated uses ATP; gated uses phagocytosis
options.C: Ungated exports proteins; gated exports bacteria
options.D: Ungated sits in nuclei; gated sits in lysosomes

questions.explanation: Gated channels switch states in response to voltage changes or ligand binding.

questions.question: A ligand-gated channel opens when:

options.D: A specific chemical ligand binds to it

questions.explanation: Chemical messenger binding triggers conformational gating.

questions.question: Once a voltage-gated channel opens, the ion direction through it is governed by:
questions.explanation: Channel flux remains passive and follows the electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: Vesicular transport consumes cellular energy and requires specialized membrane machinery.
questions.explanation: As listed in the chapter overview table, vesicular movement requires cellular energy and machinery.

questions.question: Why can facilitated diffusion NOT climb indefinitely as extracellular glucose rises:

options.A: Carrier binding sites and turnover rates reach saturation
options.C: Glucose becomes lipid-soluble at high concentration
options.D: ATP reserves run out inside the carrier

questions.explanation: Finite carrier number caps the maximal transport velocity (Vmax behavior).

questions.question: How do simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion compare regarding energy and gradient:

options.A: Simple is passive; facilitated is primary active
options.B: Simple uses ATP; facilitated uses stored Na+ gradients
options.C: Both are passive and move down gradients without direct ATP

questions.explanation: Both mechanisms remain passive despite differing in carrier involvement and saturation.

questions.question: Which change would REDUCE passive diffusion rate across an epithelial barrier:

options.B: Doubling membrane thickness while halving concentration difference

questions.explanation: Thicker diffusion distance and a shallower gradient both slow net flux.

questions.question: Which set of conditions yields the FASTEST passive diffusion of a solute:

options.A: Large gradient, high permeability, thin membrane, small solute
options.B: Small gradient, low permeability, thick barrier, large solute
options.C: Opposing electrical force, cold temperature, thick barrier
options.D: Large molecule, zero gradient, high viscosity

questions.explanation: All four favorable conditions accelerate simple diffusion rate.

questions.question: How does FILTRATION differ from simple solute diffusion:

options.A: Individual solutes move solely by random lipid solubility without pressure
options.B: Water moves toward higher protein concentration without pressure
options.D: Hydrostatic pressure drives bulk fluid and dissolved solutes together across a barrier

questions.explanation: Filtration is pressure-driven bulk movement across porous barriers such as glomerular capillaries.

questions.question: If extracellular fluid becomes markedly more concentrated with non-penetrating solutes than cytosol, water undergoes:
questions.explanation: Water flows osmotically toward the higher effective solute concentration outside.

questions.question: Increasing effective intracellular non-penetrating solute concentration favors:
questions.explanation: Higher effective intracellular osmotic strength draws water inward.

questions.question: Which process moves cargo OUT of a cell across the plasma membrane:
questions.explanation: All three endocytic routes move cargo inward; exocytosis releases cargo outward.

questions.question: Increasing membrane thickness accelerates passive solute diffusion rate across the lipid bilayer.
questions.explanation: Greater membrane thickness lengthens diffusion distance and slows passive diffusion.

questions.question: Why is plasma ONCOTIC pressure (~25 mmHg) essential clinically:

options.A: It acts as the primary ATP source for Na+/K+-ATPase
options.B: It exerts an osmotic pull retaining fluid due to plasma proteins
options.C: It triggers phagocytosis by red blood cells
options.D: It pumps H+ ions into urine

questions.explanation: Plasma proteins remain mostly intravascular, creating colloid osmotic pressure.

questions.question: Comparing osmotic pressure with filtration: filtration depends on hydrostatic pressure, whereas osmosis depends on:

options.D: Effective osmotic solute difference across a selective barrier

questions.explanation: Water moves down its own water-potential/osmotic gradient across semipermeable barriers.

questions.question: How does a carrier transporter relocate solutes after binding them:

options.A: It dissolves completely out of the bilayer
options.B: It opens a non-selective tear in phospholipids
options.C: Conformational shape change exposes the binding site to the opposite face
options.D: It converts into a clathrin vesicle

questions.explanation: Alternating conformational access releases bound solute on the opposite side.

questions.question: Why does the Na+/K+-ATPase contribute directly to resting membrane electrical potential:

options.A: It pumps 3 positive charges out for every 2 positive charges in per cycle
options.B: It exports negative chloride ions via clathrin
options.C: It equilibrates Na+ and K+ equally at 1:1
options.D: It brings large negatively charged proteins into the cell

questions.explanation: A net export of +1 charge per ATP cycle makes the pump electrogenic.

questions.question: What would happen rapidly to transmembrane Na+ and K+ gradients if cellular ATP production failed:

options.A: Primary active transport would speed up
options.B: Na+/K+-ATPase would stop and ion gradients would run down
options.C: Intracellular K+ would rise higher above normal
options.D: Secondary Na+/glucose transport would intensify permanently

questions.explanation: ATP depletion halts primary pumps, dissipating ion gradients.

questions.question: Which combination correctly pairs a transporter class with its stoichiometry direction:

options.A: Uniport: 2 solutes same direction; Symport: 1 solute
options.B: Antiport: 1 solute one way; Uniport: 2 solutes opposite ways
options.C: Symport: 1 solute; Antiport: passive water only
options.D: Symport: 2 solutes same direction; Antiport: 2 solutes opposite directions

questions.explanation: Uniport=1 solute; symport=2 same way; antiport=2 opposite ways.

questions.question: Which transport mechanism could NEVER move a solute uphill against its electrochemical gradient:
questions.explanation: Without coupling to ATP or a second solute's gradient, a passive uniporter only moves downhill.

questions.question: Colloid osmotic pressure and oncotic pressure refer to the osmotic effect contributed by blood plasma proteins.
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins behave as colloids generating ~25 mmHg oncotic pressure.

questions.question: Symporters move two different solutes in opposite directions across the plasma membrane.
questions.explanation: Moving two solutes in opposite directions is antiport (counter-transport), not symport.

questions.question: In secondary active Na+/glucose co-transport, why does glucose move UPHILL:

options.A: It couples to Na+ moving downhill along a gradient built by Na+/K+-ATPase
options.B: The symporter hydrolyzes two ATP molecules per glucose
options.C: Glucose diffuses passively from high luminal concentration only
options.D: Hydrostatic blood pressure pushes glucose backward

questions.explanation: Energy stored in the inward Na+ gradient drives uphill glucose co-transport.

questions.question: What happens to Na+/Ca2+ counter-transport if extracellular Na+ is depleted or the Na+ gradient collapses:

options.B: Secondary Ca2+ extrusion via Na+/Ca2+ exchange is impaired
options.D: Calcium stops needing any active transport

questions.explanation: Secondary exchangers rely directly on the transmembrane sodium gradient.

questions.question: Which ion pumps actively lower intracellular Ca2+ or transfer protons directly using ATP:
questions.explanation: Ca2+-ATPases and H+-ATPases are primary active pumps alongside Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.question: Why is calling a sodium-glucose symporter a 'primary ATP pump' an exam error:

options.B: The symporter does not hydrolyze ATP itself; it uses a secondary Na+ gradient
options.D: It requires clathrin rather than a protein carrier

questions.explanation: The chapter highlights this distinction explicitly under Common Exam Trap.

questions.question: How does Na+/H+ counter-transport differ directionally from Na+/amino acid co-transport:

options.A: Both move Na+ downhill, but H+ goes opposite to Na+ whereas amino acids move with Na+
options.B: Na+/H+ uses ATP directly while amino acids use vesicles
options.C: H+ diffuses through lipids while Na+ uses phagocytosis
options.D: Both carry solutes out of the cell via exocytosis

questions.explanation: Co-transport moves solutes together; counter-transport exchanges them in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which set lists ONLY secondary active processes from page 5:
questions.explanation: All primary ATPases use ATP directly, whereas symport/antiport couples use stored Na+ gradients.

questions.question: All active transport of Cl-, Ca2+, H+, Na+, and K+ occurs by the single same protein molecule.
questions.explanation: Different dedicated primary pumps and secondary carriers handle different ions across membranes.

questions.question: Stopping Na+/K+-ATPase indirectly impairs secondary active transport of glucose and amino acids.
questions.explanation: Without Na+/K+-ATPase maintaining the low intracellular Na+ gradient, Na+-linked secondary transport fails.

questions.question: How does pinocytosis differ structurally and functionally from receptor-mediated endocytosis:

options.A: Pinocytosis exports enzymes; receptor-mediated imports bacteria
options.B: Pinocytosis non-selectively samples fluid droplets; receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates ligands on receptors
options.C: Pinocytosis requires phagosomes; receptor-mediated uses connexons
options.D: Pinocytosis is passive osmosis; receptor-mediated uses filtration

questions.explanation: Surface receptor binding gives receptor-mediated endocytosis high selectivity.

questions.question: Why does a macrophage enclose a bacterium in a PHAGOSOME before digestion:

options.A: To isolate the large particle inside a vesicle that fuses with lysosomal enzymes
options.B: To push the bacterium through a channel pore
options.C: To allow clathrin to dissolve the bacterium without lysosomes
options.D: To move the bacterium by secondary Na+ antiport

questions.explanation: Phagosome-lysosome fusion confines destructive digestive enzymes away from cytosol.

questions.question: If a cell lacks CLATHRIN coat proteins, which step of receptor-mediated endocytosis is disrupted:

options.B: Direct primary ATP pumping of 3 Na+ out
options.C: Coated-pit invagination and vesicle formation around receptor-ligand complexes

questions.explanation: Clathrin assembles the coat that bends receptor-rich membrane pits into vesicles.

questions.question: Which mistake confuses CLATHRIN with another component of receptor-mediated endocytosis:

options.A: Calling clathrin a membrane coating protein
options.B: Saying clathrin participates in vesicle invagination
options.C: Recognizing that ligands bind surface receptors
options.D: Calling clathrin the ligand receptor instead of the coat protein

questions.explanation: Clathrin forms the vesicle coat; separate transmembrane proteins serve as ligand receptors.

questions.question: How does TRANSCYTOSIS achieve directional transport across an endothelial barrier cell:

options.A: Uptake by endocytosis at one cell face
options.B: Intracellular vesicle transit and exocytosis at the opposite face
options.C: Channel opening to allow whole red cells through cytosol

questions.explanation: Transcytosis couples endocytosis on one pole with exocytosis on the opposite pole.

questions.question: Following pinocytosis of extracellular fluid, engulfed vesicles typically deliver cargo toward:
questions.explanation: Pinocytic vesicles enter the intracellular endosomal-lysosomal pathway.

questions.question: Secretion of a synthesized peptide product out of a gland cell uses:
questions.explanation: Secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane to release cargo by exocytosis.

questions.question: A molecule is too large for carriers and lacks a specific surface receptor; how might a cell still internalize dissolved traces of it:
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis nonspecifically samples small droplets of surrounding extracellular fluid.

questions.question: Renal glomerular filtration moves fluid across capillary walls via hydrostatic pressure gradients.
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure drives bulk filtration across glomerular and capillary barriers.

questions.question: During pinocytosis, clathrin receptors bind solid bacteria inside phagosomes for outward exocytosis.
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis takes up small droplets of extracellular fluid inward without forming bacterial phagosomes.

questions.question: Which transport mechanism moves glucose DOWN its concentration gradient via a saturable membrane protein:
questions.explanation: Glucose carriers facilitate downhill movement and display saturation kinetics.

questions.question: What characterizes the direction and energy source of PRIMARY active transport:

options.A: Uphill movement powered directly by ATP
options.C: Uphill movement powered solely by hydrostatic pressure
options.D: Bulk vesicle entry powered by osmosis

questions.explanation: Primary pumps spend ATP directly to move solutes against gradients.

questions.question: If an uncharged solute has equal concentration on both sides of a membrane, net simple diffusion is:
questions.explanation: With no concentration difference on an uncharged particle, forward and backward fluxes balance.

questions.question: Why do water-soluble ions pass poorly through pure phospholipid tails without channels:

options.C: They require an aqueous transmembrane path supplied by channel proteins
options.D: Ions are always trapped in phagosomes

questions.explanation: Hydrophobic membrane cores block bare ions, so aqueous protein channels mediate passage.

questions.question: At very high extracellular solute concentration, why does simple diffusion keep rising linearly while facilitated diffusion plateaus:

options.A: Simple diffusion lacks saturable protein binding sites
options.C: Simple diffusion generates its own ATP

questions.explanation: Without finite binding pockets, lipid diffusion rate remains proportional to the gradient.

questions.question: Increasing which variable SLOWS solute diffusion across a biological membrane:
questions.explanation: Greater thickness increases path length and slows flux.

questions.question: How do bulk flow and simple diffusion fundamentally differ:

options.A: Bulk flow burns ATP directly; diffusion uses vesicles
options.B: Bulk flow moves fluid via pressure; diffusion moves solutes via concentration
options.C: Bulk flow happens only in nuclei; diffusion in blood
options.D: Bulk flow carries zero dissolved electrolytes or ions

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure drives collective fluid movement in filtration/bulk flow.

questions.question: Plasma oncotic pressure of ~25 mmHg opposes excessive fluid loss out of capillaries driven by:
questions.explanation: Plasma protein osmotic draw opposes capillary hydrostatic filtration.

questions.question: Putting red cells into a solution with MUCH HIGHER effective solute concentration causes water to move by:
questions.explanation: Water shifts toward the compartment with greater effective osmotic solute concentration.

questions.question: Which directional relationship defines a SYMPORTER:

options.B: Two solutes move in the same direction
options.C: Two solutes move in opposite directions

questions.explanation: Symporters mediate co-transport in the same direction.

questions.question: Which directional relationship defines an ANTIPORTER:

options.B: One ion diffuses through an ungated pore
options.D: Two solutes move in opposite directions

questions.explanation: Antiporters exchange solutes in opposite directions.

questions.question: Each turn of the Na+/K+-ATPase transfers:
questions.explanation: Unequal 3:2 cation pumping maintains ionic gradients and contributes resting electrogenicity.

questions.question: Because Na+/K+-ATPase moves 3 positive ions out and only 2 in, each cycle moves:
questions.explanation: The pump exports one net +1 charge per cycle.

questions.question: Which ion pump clears Ca2+ from cytosol to maintain low intracellular Ca2+ levels:
questions.explanation: ATP-driven Ca2+ pumps move Ca2+ out of cytosol across cell or organelle membranes.

questions.question: Why is secondary active transport still fundamentally ENERGY-DEPENDENT:

options.A: Every symporter binds ATP on its cytoplasmic tail
options.B: It relies exclusively on heat from filtration
options.D: It relies on an ion gradient built by ATP-driven primary pumps

questions.explanation: Collapsing the primary pump collapses the driving ion gradient.

questions.question: Which pair contrasts CO-TRANSPORT and COUNTER-TRANSPORT examples accurately:
questions.explanation: Glucose moves with Na+ (symport), whereas Ca2+ or H+ exchanges opposite to Na+ (antiport).

questions.question: Which mechanism allows a cell to internalize extracellular fluid drops without binding a specific ligand receptor:
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis non-selectively engulfs small aliquots of extracellular fluid.

questions.question: Phagocytosis differs from pinocytosis in cargo scale and cell specialization because phagocytosis:

options.A: Takes up dissolved gases in erythrocytes
options.C: Engulfs large particles such as microbes mainly in neutrophils and macrophages
options.D: Relies on clathrin-coated fluid droplets only

questions.explanation: Immune phagocytes surround large particulate cargo inside a phagosome.

questions.question: After macrophage phagocytosis encloses cellular debris, degradation occurs when:
questions.explanation: Lysosomal fusion introduces digestive hydrolases into the phagosome.

questions.question: Why is receptor-mediated endocytosis vital for selective macromolecular uptake:

options.A: Ligands bind matching surface receptors before clathrin-coated vesicle formation
options.B: It relies on simple lipid diffusion of large proteins
options.C: It pulls fluid indiscriminately by bulk pressure
options.D: It pushes all cargo through narrow ion channels

questions.explanation: Receptor recognition selectively concentrates specific extracellular molecules.

questions.question: During receptor-mediated endocytosis, receptor-ligand complexes collect into:

options.D: A clathrin-coated membrane region that invaginates

questions.explanation: Coated pits invaginate to form selective intracellular transport vesicles.

questions.question: Transporting intact plasma antibodies across an endothelial cell wall from one side to the other uses:
questions.explanation: Transcytosis couples endocytosis on one cell face with exocytosis on the opposite face.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly traces TRANSCYTOSIS across a barrier cell:

options.A: Exocytosis on face 1 -> phagocytosis -> simple diffusion on face 2
options.B: Endocytosis on face 1 -> intracellular vesicle transit -> exocytosis on face 2
options.C: Primary ATP pump -> channel gating -> filtration

questions.explanation: Cargo traverses the cell inside a vesicle between opposite membranes.

questions.question: Which pairing in the vesicular summary table is accurate:

options.A: Pinocytosis -> fluid-phase uptake; Exocytosis -> release of secretory product
options.B: Phagocytosis -> outward hormone secretion; Transcytosis -> water osmosis
options.C: Exocytosis -> bacterial engulfment; Pinocytosis -> macromolecule exit

questions.explanation: Pinocytosis imports fluid, while exocytosis exports secretory vesicles.

questions.question: Which statement best separates FACILITATED diffusion from ACTIVE transport:

options.A: Facilitated diffusion uses ATP; active transport never does
options.B: Facilitated diffusion moves only ions; active moves only gases
options.D: Facilitated diffusion is downhill and never concentrates a solute against its gradient

questions.explanation: Carriers exist in both, but only active transport pumps uphill against gradients.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT slow passive diffusion:

options.D: Opposing electrical forces on an ion

questions.explanation: Warming increases molecular kinetic energy and favors faster diffusion.

questions.question: Glomerular filtration in the kidney illustrates fluid and small-solute movement driven by:

options.D: Osmotic pull into Bowman space by hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Glomerular capillaries use blood pressure gradients for bulk filtration.

questions.question: Which ion is actively maintained at HIGH concentration INSIDE the cell relative to ECF:
questions.explanation: Na+/K+-ATPase keeps intracellular K+ high while Ca2+-ATPases keep cytosolic Ca2+ very low.

questions.question: In an antiport exchanger moving Na+ inward and H+ outward, which solute drives the uphill step:

options.A: ATP binds H+ directly inside the antiporter
options.B: Downhill Na+ entry powers uphill H+ extrusion
options.C: H+ diffuses downhill to push Na+ into the nucleus

questions.explanation: The primary Na+ gradient energizes uphill H+ counter-transport.

questions.question: Which vesicular step releases stored neurotransmitter or hormone from vesicles:
questions.explanation: Vesicle-plasma membrane fusion discharges secretory cargo outward.

questions.question: Why are neutrophils and macrophages highlighted in vesicular transport:

options.A: They perform phagocytosis to clear microbes and debris
options.C: They use clathrin exclusively for O2 transport

questions.explanation: These immune defenders are specialized phagocytes.

questions.question: What distinguishes osmotic pressure from hydrostatic filtration pressure conceptually:

options.A: Osmotic pressure moves solids only; hydrostatic stops water completely
options.B: Osmotic pressure applies only to gases
options.C: Osmotic pressure prevents water movement caused by solute differences; hydrostatic pressure drives bulk flow

questions.explanation: Osmotic draw reflects solute concentration difference; hydrostatic force pushes fluid physically.

questions.question: If a cell binds a specific ligand on its receptor and internalizes it via a coated pit, the coat protein is:
questions.explanation: Clathrin forms the characteristic coat during pit invagination.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY passive processes:

options.A: Simple diffusion, channel diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis

questions.explanation: Diffusion, channels, facilitated carriers, and osmosis require no direct ATP or active uphill pumping.

questions.question: Why do channel proteins still qualify as passive when gated by voltage:

options.A: Voltage transfers ATP molecules onto every ion
options.B: Voltage opens the gate, but net ion flux still follows the electrochemical gradient
options.D: Voltage converts the pore into an antiporter

questions.explanation: Gating regulates permeability, not the thermodynamic direction of flow.

questions.question: Which statement summarizes 'passive vs active vs vesicular' accurately:

options.A: Passive = uphill; vesicular = lipid diffusion only
options.D: Passive = downhill; primary active = ATP pump; secondary = stored ion gradient; vesicular = bulk membrane sacs

questions.explanation: This matches the chapter's One-Minute Review framework.

questions.question: In Na+/K+-ATPase, how do pumped ion counts differ per cycle:

options.A: 2 Na+ pumped out vs 3 K+ pumped in
options.B: 3 Ca2+ pumped out vs 2 H+ pumped in
options.C: 3 Na+ pumped out vs 2 K+ pumped in

questions.explanation: The pump transfers 3 Na+ outward and 2 K+ inward per ATP cycle.

questions.question: Which tissues secrete acid actively using proton-pumping ATPases:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen-ion pumps transfer protons across membranes where acid transport is required.

questions.question: Why is clathrin NOT classified as the hormone receptor in selective endocytosis:

options.A: Clathrin hydrolyzes ATP for Na+ uptake
options.B: Clathrin coats the invaginating pit; transmembrane receptors bind ligands
options.C: Clathrin diffuses freely as an O2 carrier

questions.explanation: Ligands bind specific surface receptors while clathrin forms the coating scaffold.

questions.question: Which five ions are grouped under active transport mechanisms in the chapter:

options.C: Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl-

questions.explanation: The source highlights Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- among actively transported ions.

questions.question: Carrier saturation can occur in both facilitated diffusion and carrier-mediated active transport because both have finite binding sites.
questions.explanation: Any protein carrier with finite binding sites and conformational turnover rate exhibits saturation.

questions.question: Exosmosis refers to net water movement INTO a cell when placed in dilute solution.
questions.explanation: Entry of water is endosmosis; exit of water is exosmosis.

questions.question: Transcytosis transports cargo across an endothelial barrier without mixing it directly with simple lipid diffusion.
questions.explanation: Cargo stays enclosed inside vesicles from uptake at one side to release at the other.

questions.question: Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires clathrin to act as the actual hormone-binding receptor.
questions.explanation: Clathrin is a cytoplasmic coat protein; specific membrane receptors bind the ligands.

questions.question: Antiporters and symporters are both types of coupled multi-solute transporters.
questions.explanation: Both move two different solute species either in opposite directions (antiport) or the same direction (symport).

questions.question: Calcium ATPases raise cytosolic Ca2+ concentration rapidly during resting states.
questions.explanation: Calcium ATPases lower cytosolic Ca2+ concentration by pumping it across membranes.

questions.question: During simple diffusion, higher lipid solubility generally favors faster passage through the bilayer.
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble small solutes dissolve through the phospholipid core more rapidly.

questions.question: Bulk flow moves fluid strictly from lower hydrostatic pressure toward higher hydrostatic pressure.
questions.explanation: Bulk flow drives fluid down a pressure gradient, from higher to lower hydrostatic pressure.

questions.question: Phagocytosis brings in dissolved fluid droplets too small to see, whereas pinocytosis engulfs whole bacteria.
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid droplets; phagocytosis engulfs large particles like microbes.

questions.question: Both endocytosis and exocytosis depend on membrane-bounded vesicles and cellular energy.
questions.explanation: Vesicular budding, trafficking, and fusion require cellular machinery and energy.

questions.question: A researcher blocks ALL cellular ATP production instantaneously while leaving membranes intact. Which mechanism STILL operates immediately down pre-existing gradients until gradients decay:

options.B: Primary Na+/K+-ATPase ion pumping against gradients
options.C: Active vesicular exocytosis of new secretory cargo

questions.explanation: Passive diffusion and channels follow existing gradients without direct ATP, whereas primary pumps and vesicle export fail without ATP.

questions.question: Why does adding an electrical charge to a solute alter its passive transport behavior compared with glucose:

options.A: The molecule switches immediately to phagocytosis
options.D: Both concentration difference and membrane voltage now determine its net driving force

questions.explanation: Ions obey the electrochemical gradient rather than concentration alone.

questions.question: If a voltage-gated Na+ channel opens in a resting cell (ECF Na+-rich, interior negative), Na+ rushes inward by:

options.B: Passive diffusion down its electrochemical gradient

questions.explanation: Even though voltage triggers the gate, ion flow through the open aqueous pore is passive.

questions.question: Why can lipid-soluble CO2 cross membranes rapidly without channel gating whereas water and ions lean on membrane proteins:

options.A: CO2 is pumped outward through clathrin coats
options.B: Water is much larger than plasma albumin proteins
options.C: Nonpolar CO2 dissolves in lipids; water and ions need aqueous pores
options.D: Ions cannot dissolve in extracellular water

questions.explanation: Chemical polarity dictates bilayer vs aqueous-channel reliance.

questions.question: If an experimental toxin inserts a membrane pump that drives solute X uphill using direct ATP hydrolysis, why is X no longer passive:

options.A: Open voltage-gated channels allow passive diffusion
options.B: Active ATP coupling reverses net downhill gradient movement
options.C: Lipid-soluble gases diffuse down partial pressures
options.D: Carriers facilitate downhill glucose entry without ATP

questions.explanation: Passive mechanisms never push solutes uphill against net driving forces.

questions.question: Suppose ATP is consumed during a transport step, yet the transporter protein moving solute X does NOT possess an ATPase site. Most likely X moves by:

options.A: Secondary active transport or vesicular machinery

questions.explanation: Indirect energy reliance characterizes secondary active gradients (from primary pumps) and energized vesicular trafficking.

questions.question: Comparing an ungated channel with a carrier performing facilitated diffusion: both remain passive, yet ONLY the carrier:

options.A: Moves solutes uphill directly with ATP hydrolysis
options.C: Operates solely via capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.D: Requires conformational cycling per bound solute

questions.explanation: Channels form continuous aqueous pores when open, whereas carriers bind and undergo conformational cycles.

questions.question: Even when an ion moves DOWN its concentration gradient, a sufficiently strong opposing electrical gradient can halt or reverse net passive movement.
questions.explanation: Net passive driving force on an ion equals the combined electrochemical gradient, not concentration alone.

questions.question: Two tissues express glucose carriers with equal turnover speed per carrier, but Tissue A has 5x more carriers than Tissue B. Under saturating glucose:

options.A: Both tissues saturate at the exact same maximal rate
options.B: Tissue A achieves a higher maximal transport plateau
options.C: Tissue A converts facilitated transport into phagocytosis
options.D: Tissue B stops showing saturation kinetics

questions.explanation: Maximal facilitated transport rate depends on the total number of membrane carriers available.

questions.question: A drug selectively blocks carrier conformational cycling without piercing the phospholipid bilayer. Which process is severely impaired while O2 exchange stays normal:
questions.explanation: Carriers are essential for facilitated diffusion, whereas small gases cross phospholipids directly.

questions.question: Which experimental graph best distinguishes facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion as extracellular solute rises:

options.A: Simple diffusion plateaus while facilitated drops to zero
options.B: Both freeze at zero flux until ATP is added
options.C: Facilitated diffusion plateaus while simple diffusion rises linearly
options.D: Both reverse direction whenever temperature rises

questions.explanation: Limited carrier binding sites produce hyperbolic saturation in facilitated diffusion.

questions.question: A pathological edema thickens the alveolar-capillary barrier AND lowers alveolar O2 gradient. What happens to O2 diffusion rate:

options.B: Both changes reduce passive diffusion rate
options.C: Only filtration changes; diffusion stays unchanged

questions.explanation: Greater diffusion distance and smaller driving gradient act additively to slow diffusion.

questions.question: Which clinical situation directly exemplifies hydrostatic FILTRATION rather than pure solute diffusion or osmosis:

options.A: O2 entering erythrocytes down a concentration gradient
options.B: Water shrinking an RBC in concentrated saline
options.D: Blood pressure forcing plasma fluid across renal glomeruli

questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration uses hydrostatic pressure gradients for bulk fluid-and-solute movement.

questions.question: A cell shrinks via EXOSMOSIS after immersion in hypertonic medium; what membrane gradient reversed if adding extracellular water makes it swell next:

options.A: Effective solute concentration outside dropped below cytosol
options.B: Carrier saturation velocity exceeded Vmax outside
options.C: Hydrostatic capillary filtration pushed glucose inside

questions.explanation: Osmosis moves water toward the higher effective osmotic concentration across a selective barrier.

questions.question: Wait: if cell B is placed in pure distilled water (near-zero effective extracellular solute), net water direction is:
questions.explanation: Water shifts toward the higher effective intracellular solute concentration (endosmosis).

questions.question: Increasing solute molecular radius while simultaneously lowering membrane temperature will affect passive diffusion by:
questions.explanation: Larger size and lower thermal energy both reduce diffusion velocity.

questions.question: When all facilitated-diffusion carriers are 100% saturated, doubling the extracellular glucose gradient immediately doubles transport velocity.
questions.explanation: Finite binding sites and turnover speed cap facilitated transport at saturation.

questions.question: Why does the chapter specify EFFECTIVE concentration of water-attracting solutes in defining osmosis rather than total solute mass:

options.A: Small gases determine 100% of oncotic pressure
options.B: Proteins pass faster than water through channels
options.C: Osmosis depends solely on hydrostatic pump cycles
options.D: Only solutes restricted by the selective barrier establish sustained osmotic water draw

questions.explanation: Selectively retained solutes create effective osmotic gradients across the membrane.

questions.question: If a membrane transporter binds one solute at a time, flips conformation, and releases it down its gradient, it is simultaneously a:
questions.explanation: Uniporters carry a single solute type and mediate passive facilitated diffusion when downhill.

questions.question: Suppose the Na+/K+-ATPase mutated to import 3 K+ for every 3 Na+ exported per ATP. How would its direct electrical behavior change:

options.A: It would pump double the net positive charge outward
options.B: Its direct net charge transfer per cycle would fall from +1 outward to zero (electroneutral)
options.C: It would reverse intracellular K+ to near zero
options.D: It would become a secondary symporter

questions.explanation: Normal 3 Na+ out / 2 K+ in exports +1 net charge; 3:3 exchange would transfer zero net charge.

questions.question: What is the immediate functional link between Na+/K+-ATPase (page 4) and ALL secondary Na+-coupled transporters (page 5):

options.A: Na+/K+-ATPase coats vesicles with clathrin for symporters
options.B: Secondary transporters donate ATP back to Na+/K+-ATPase
options.C: Na+/K+-ATPase maintains low cytosolic Na+, preserving the inward Na+ gradient used as fuel

questions.explanation: Primary active extrusion of Na+ stores potential energy in the inward Na+ gradient.

questions.question: Compare a symporter and an antiporter under complete loss of the driving ion gradient: both fail to pump their target solute uphill because:

options.B: Only uniporters survive ATP depletion forever
options.D: Neither possesses direct ATP hydrolysis to power uphill transport alone

questions.explanation: Secondary transporters depend entirely on the driving gradient rather than direct ATP cleavage.

questions.question: Which statement accurately distinguishes OSMOTIC pressure from ONCOTIC pressure:

options.A: Osmotic pressure prevents net osmosis from any solutes; oncotic pressure specifically measures the ~25 mmHg osmotic effect of colloidal plasma proteins
options.B: Oncotic pressure is always 10x larger than capillary blood pressure
options.C: Osmotic pressure applies only to vesicles; oncotic applies only to phagocytosis
options.D: Oncotic pressure moves Na+ via symport

questions.explanation: Oncotic pressure is the colloidal/plasma-protein subset of total osmotic pressure.

questions.question: A clinician notes that fluid filtration across a capillary bed suddenly rises because plasma protein concentration fell sharply. Which value dropped below normal:
questions.explanation: Loss of plasma proteins lowers colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure.

questions.question: Because Na+/K+-ATPase moves both Na+ and K+ against their gradients simultaneously using ATP, it is a primary active antiporter-type pump.
questions.explanation: It directly hydrolyzes ATP to exchange 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in against their gradients.

questions.question: All uniporters hydrolyze ATP directly because they undergo conformational shape changes.
questions.explanation: Conformational cycling occurs in passive facilitated diffusion uniporters too, without ATP.

questions.question: An inhibitor specifically poisons Na+/K+-ATPase (ouabain-like effect) without directly binding the Na+/glucose symporter or Na+/Ca2+ antiporter. What happens next:

options.A: Na+/glucose uptake accelerates because it hydrolyzes ATP directly
options.B: Cytosolic Ca2+ falls even lower via Na+/Ca2+ exchange
options.C: Both Na+/glucose uptake and Na+/Ca2+ exchange fail secondarily as intracellular Na+ builds up
options.D: H+ pumps convert into simple O2 diffusion

questions.explanation: Because both secondary transporters rely on the low intracellular Na+ gradient maintained by Na+/K+-ATPase, poisoning the primary pump cripples them.

questions.question: Which contrast correctly identifies a PRIMARY ATP pump vs a SECONDARY coupled transporter:

options.A: Ca2+-ATPase uses ATP directly; Na+/H+ exchanger uses the Na+ gradient
options.B: Na+/glucose symporter uses ATP directly; Na+/K+-ATPase uses Na+ gradient
options.C: Clathrin uses ATP to carry amino acids; H+-ATPase uses osmosis
options.D: Phagosome = primary active; exocytosis = secondary active

questions.explanation: Ca2+-ATPase and H+-ATPase are primary pumps; Na+/H+ and Na+/glucose are secondary.

questions.question: Why does intracellular [Ca2+] remain dramatically lower than extracellular [Ca2+] despite continuous cellular signaling:

options.A: Ca2+ is membrane-permeable like O2 and leaves freely by simple diffusion
options.B: Combined action of primary Ca2+-ATPases and secondary Na+/Ca2+ counter-transport removes cytosolic Ca2+
options.D: Hydrostatic blood pressure filters Ca2+ out of mitochondria

questions.explanation: Both ATP-driven Ca2+ pumps and Na+/Ca2+ exchangers extrude or sequester Ca2+.

questions.question: If extracellular [Na+] is artificially replaced with an impermeant cation, which pair of transport processes stops working effectively:

options.D: Secondary Na+/amino acid co-transport and Na+/Ca2+ counter-transport

questions.explanation: Both co-transport and counter-transport driven by inward Na+ influx require an extracellular Na+ driving gradient.

questions.question: Which statement exposes the classic 'Common Exam Trap' about intestinal/renal glucose absorption via SGLT-type Na+/glucose symport:

options.A: It never depends on energy anywhere in the cell
options.B: It moves glucose uphill without direct ATP hydrolysis at the symporter itself
options.C: It exchanges glucose outward in antiport with K+
options.D: It relies solely on simple diffusion through phospholipids

questions.explanation: It is energy-dependent secondarily, not primary ATPase-driven.

questions.question: Which ion movement direction matches Na+/H+ counter-transport during acid extrusion:

options.A: Both Na+ and H+ enter the cell together
options.B: H+ diffuses inward by osmosis while Na+ exits by pinocytosis
options.C: Na+ moves into the cell down its gradient while H+ moves out against its gradient

questions.explanation: Antiport couples downhill Na+ entry to uphill H+ export.

questions.question: If a cell lacks ATP, secondary active transport fails immediately even before the Na+ gradient dissipates.
questions.explanation: Secondary transport continues briefly as long as the pre-existing Na+ gradient persists, failing once that gradient runs down.

questions.question: Active transport involves Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- through dedicated primary or secondary mechanisms rather than simple uncoupled diffusion.
questions.explanation: The sheet identifies all five among ions managed by active transport pathways.

questions.question: A mutant endothelial cell forms normal phagosomes and normal exocytic vesicles, yet fails to deliver a specific plasma ligand across the capillary wall. If ligand-receptor binding fails OR clathrin coating fails, which pathway breaks:
questions.explanation: Selective uptake across endothelium depends on receptor recognition and coated-vesicle internalization.

questions.question: Why is calling CLATHRIN 'the LDL or hormone receptor' scientifically incorrect:

options.A: Clathrin sits inside lysosomes as an acid hydrolase
options.B: Clathrin channels 3 Na+ out per cycle
options.C: Clathrin is a lipid component of cholesterol
options.D: Receptors bind specific extracellular ligands; clathrin forms the membrane-bending protein coat on the pit

questions.explanation: Receptors recognize ligands; clathrin coats the invaginating pit.

questions.question: Which experimental comparison proves phagocytosis and pinocytosis are distinct despite both being endocytosis:

options.A: Phagocytosis moves fluid outward; pinocytosis moves proteins outward
options.B: Phagocytosis engulfs large particles in phagosomes; pinocytosis drinks fluid
options.C: Pinocytosis uses clathrin hormone receptors for every single water molecule
options.D: Phagocytosis destroys internalized bacteria without any lysosomal fusion

questions.explanation: Cargo scale, membrane projections, phagosome formation, and phagocyte specialization distinguish them.

questions.question: Suppose lysosomal fusion is genetically blocked in a neutrophil. After engulfing bacteria, what accumulates intact inside the cell:
questions.explanation: Engulfment into phagosomes succeeds, but digestion fails without lysosomal enzyme delivery.

questions.question: Why does TRANSCYTOSIS preserve directionality across an epithelial or endothelial cell:

options.A: Cargo diffuses freely across tight junctions and cytoplasm
options.B: Na+/K+-ATPase pumps plasma proteins straight through nuclear pores
options.C: Vesicles endocytose at one pole and exocytose at the opposite
options.D: Phagosomes burst inside the cytosol before reaching opposite faces

questions.explanation: Enclosure inside directed vesicles moves macromolecular cargo cleanly across barrier cells.

questions.question: Which sequence contrasts ALL FOUR major membrane transport families in exact order: gradient-driven carrier -> ATP pump -> gradient-coupled uphill carrier -> vesicle engulfment:

options.A: Simple diffusion -> secondary active -> filtration -> exocytosis
options.B: Facilitated diffusion -> primary active -> secondary active -> endocytosis
options.C: Osmosis -> facilitated diffusion -> primary active -> uniport

questions.explanation: This matches passive carrier, direct ATP pump, indirect ion-gradient carrier, and vesicular entry.

questions.question: A pancreatic cell secretes digestive zymogens packaged in Golgi vesicles. What prevents massive permanent swelling of the plasma membrane surface over time if exocytosis stayed unmatched:

options.A: Balanced inward membrane retrieval via endocytosis
options.B: Reverse simple diffusion of phospholipids out to air
options.C: Conversion of bilayers into H+ pumps

questions.explanation: Endocytosis and exocytosis recycle membrane area dynamically.

questions.question: Because transcytosis ends with vesicle fusion at the opposite cell surface, it requires zero cellular energy.
questions.explanation: Like other vesicular processes, transcytosis requires cellular energy and membrane-trafficking machinery.

questions.question: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, what ensures that scarce extracellular molecules are internalized efficiently without drinking huge volumes of surrounding fluid:

options.A: Hydrostatic filtration pushes only that protein through lipids
options.B: Osmosis drags the ligand at 25 mmHg
options.D: High-affinity binding to matching surface receptors concentrates ligands in coated pits

questions.explanation: Surface receptor clustering concentrates specific ligands selectively.

questions.question: Endocytosis of fluid droplets (pinocytosis) exposes internalized contents to the endosomal-lysosomal pathway rather than leaving them freely dissolved in cytosol.
questions.explanation: Membrane enclosure keeps pinocytic cargo segregated within the endosomal-lysosomal system.

questions.question: An isolated cell with intact ATP and Na+/K+-ATPase is exposed to extracellular glucose PLUS a toxin collapsing ONLY the membrane Na+ gradient. Which glucose flux disappears:
questions.explanation: Secondary active Na+/glucose co-transport disappears when the Na+ gradient collapses; none of the listed passive or pinocytic fluxes rely on the Na+ gradient.

questions.question: Why can facilitated glucose carriers reach Vmax saturation while lipid-soluble O2 diffusion does not saturate:

options.A: O2 uses ATPase pumps that accelerate without limit
options.B: Carriers have finite binding sites; lipid dissolution has no protein cap
options.C: Glucose carries +3 positive charges across lipids
options.D: Lipid bilayers solidify above 25 mmHg pressure

questions.explanation: Carrier number and conformational speed limit facilitated transport.

questions.question: During nerve excitation, voltage-gated channels open and Na+ enters rapidly. Why is that inward Na+ spike STILL passive while resetting Na+ afterward is active:

options.A: Voltage-gated pores hydrolyze ATP during every influx
options.B: Resetting occurs via passive simple lipid diffusion
options.C: Influx follows the gradient; resetting pumps uphill with ATP
options.D: Influx requires phagosome fusion with lysosomes

questions.explanation: Channel opening is passive; restoring depleted ion gradients requires Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.question: If an uncharged solute diffuses passively across a membrane and temperature drops while membrane thickness doubles, net flux will:

options.A: Drop due to lower kinetic energy and longer path
options.B: Rise due to carrier site saturation

questions.explanation: Both changes decrease passive diffusion rate.

questions.question: How do capillary hydrostatic filtration pressure and plasma oncotic pressure (~25 mmHg) interact physiologically:

options.A: Both push fluid exclusively out into tissues
options.B: Hydrostatic pushes fluid out while oncotic pulls water in
options.C: Oncotic pressure pumps 3 Na+ out per cycle
options.D: Hydrostatic pressure prevents all osmosis everywhere

questions.explanation: Filtration and colloid osmotic draw oppose one another across capillary walls.

questions.question: A cell has higher effective intracellular solute concentration than surrounding fluid, yet its membrane is completely damaged and non-selective. Why will true OSMOSIS cease:

options.C: Osmosis requires a selectively permeable barrier separating effective solute differences

questions.explanation: Without selective permeability, solutes simply equilibrate rather than drawing net osmotic water.

questions.question: Why does the Na+/K+-ATPase qualify as an electrogenic primary active transporter:

options.A: It hydrolyzes ATP to pump 3 Na+ out vs 2 K+ in
options.B: It leaks K+ passively outward without spending ATP
options.C: It pumps uncharged glucose alongside chloride

questions.explanation: Direct ATP hydrolysis plus 3:2 stoichiometry produces +1 net outward charge per cycle.

questions.question: Compare Na+/K+-ATPase and H+-ATPase with Na+/glucose symport: the first two share:

options.B: Direct reliance on ATP hydrolysis to pump ions uphill

questions.explanation: Both Na+/K+ and H+ pumps are primary active ATPases.

questions.question: Why can a secondary antiporter like Na+/Ca2+ exchange move Ca2+ UPHILL out of the cell without hydrolyzing ATP itself:

options.A: Ca2+ diffuses out down a massive intracellular excess
options.B: ATP binds Ca2+ directly on the outside
options.D: Energy released as Na+ flows downhill inward drives uphill Ca2+ extrusion in the opposite direction

questions.explanation: Coupled counter-transport captures energy stored in the Na+ gradient.

questions.question: Which experimental clue proves a molecule enters via RECEPTOR-MEDIATED endocytosis rather than non-selective pinocytosis:

options.A: Uptake proceeds equally when surface receptors are digested off
options.B: Cargo crosses via simple phospholipid dissolution
options.C: Uptake depends on a matching surface receptor and concentrates into clathrin-coated pits
options.D: Cargo triggers macrophage pseudopods around 5-micrometer beads

questions.explanation: Specific receptor dependence plus coated-pit concentration defines receptor-mediated uptake.

questions.question: In neutrophils engulfing bacteria, blocking which two organelles or steps halts complete pathogen destruction sequentially:

options.A: Membrane projection engulfment (phagosome formation) -> phagosome-lysosome fusion

questions.explanation: Phagocytes first enclose cargo in a phagosome, then fuse it with lysosomes.

questions.question: In an experiment mutating the extracellular binding pocket of surface receptors while leaving intracellular clathrin intact, why does ligand endocytosis fail even though coated pits still assemble:

options.A: Clathrin directly hydrolyzes intracellular ATP to force ligands across lipid tails
options.B: Specific surface receptors must recognize ligands before clathrin-coated pits capture cargo
options.C: Clathrin functions inside phagosomes as an oxidative catalase enzyme

questions.explanation: Specific membrane receptors select extracellular ligands while clathrin forms the intracellular pit coat.

questions.question: Which process moves cargo completely ACROSS a polarized endothelial layer without releasing it free into endothelial cytosol:
questions.explanation: Transcytosis keeps macromolecules enclosed within vesicles from entry to opposite-side exocytosis.

questions.question: Suppose a toxic mutation converts an antiporter into a channel leaking both ions freely down their gradients. What capability is LOST:

options.B: Coupling downhill flux to uphill transport

questions.explanation: Free uncoupled pores cannot harvest one ion's energy to push another uphill.

questions.question: Why does active transport often display saturation just like facilitated diffusion, even though only active transport goes uphill:

options.A: Both use finite protein transporters with saturable sites
options.B: Both depend solely on hydrostatic pressure
options.C: Both move solutes exclusively inside clathrin coats
options.D: Simple diffusion saturates faster than carriers

questions.explanation: Carrier protein saturation reflects finite transporter molecules and conformational cycling time.

questions.question: Which membrane transport list uses cellular energy DIRECTLY or INDIRECTLY in EVERY listed item:

options.A: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis, filtration
options.B: Channel gating, osmosis, simple diffusion, transcytosis
options.C: Primary active, secondary active, endocytosis, exocytosis
options.D: Bulk flow, Na+/glucose symport, simple O2 diffusion

questions.explanation: Primary uses ATP directly; secondary uses ATP-built ion gradients; vesicular routes consume cellular energy.

questions.question: A cell placed in hypertonic solution shrinks via exosmosis, then slowly activates ion pumps to accumulate intracellular solutes. How will water shift next:

options.A: Water will keep leaving forever at higher speed
options.B: Water enters back into the cell by endosmosis
options.C: Plasma oncotic pressure will jump to 250 mmHg

questions.explanation: Raising effective intracellular solute concentration reverses the osmotic gradient inward.

questions.question: A capillary endothelial cell internalizes plasma macromolecules at its luminal surface normally, yet a drug blocks vesicle fusion ONLY at its abluminal pole; which process arrests at its final step:

options.A: Transcytosis across the polarized cell, leaving initial endocytosis intact
options.B: Simple diffusion directly across the hydrophobic lipid bilayer
options.C: Primary Ca2+-ATPase pumping through nuclear pores
options.D: Net water entry via selective aquaporin channels

questions.explanation: Transcytosis spans endocytosis at one surface, transcellular transit, and exocytic exit at the opposite pole.

questions.question: Why can electrical opposition slow K+ efflux even when intracellular [K+] far exceeds extracellular [K+]:

options.A: Uncharged solutes always obey membrane voltage
options.B: Membrane carriers freeze below 25 mmHg pressure
options.C: Inside-negative voltage attracts positive K+ inward
options.D: Clathrin coats block potassium pore diffusion

questions.explanation: Opposing electrical and chemical components balance within the electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: During ATP depletion, cytosolic Na+ AND Ca2+ BOTH climb above normal resting levels even before Na+/glucose carriers fail; which shared primary defect accounts for BOTH ion rises:

options.A: Failure of aquaporin water channels mediating osmotic endosmosis
options.B: Inhibition of non-selective fluid pinocytosis of glucose
options.D: Loss of direct ATP hydrolysis powering both Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+-ATPase

questions.explanation: Both Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+-ATPase are primary ATP-driven pumps maintaining low cytosolic Na+ and Ca2+.

questions.question: If clathrin-coated pits pinch off properly, yet endosomal/lysosomal fusion never happens after macrophage phagocytosis, which step succeeded:
questions.explanation: Phagosome formation precedes lysosomal fusion.

questions.question: Why is calling osmosis 'diffusion of solutes' incorrect according to the Fast Check:

options.A: Diffusion moves solutes; osmosis moves net water
options.B: Osmosis requires ATPase pumps for water entry
options.C: Solutes cannot diffuse across selective barriers
options.D: Water moves toward pure water from concentrated side

questions.explanation: Distinguishing solute flux (diffusion) from solvent flux (osmosis) avoids classic exam errors.

questions.question: A transporter moves solute A inward only when solute B exits outward, and stops when intracellular ATP and extracellular solute B are both removed. This transporter is:
questions.explanation: Opposite-direction coupled exchange dependent on a counter-ion gradient defines secondary antiport.

questions.question: What prevents simple diffusion of large polar plasma proteins across capillary endothelium by the lipid route:

options.A: Lipids pump plasma proteins out via Na+ symport
options.B: Huge size and low lipid solubility bar bilayer passage
options.C: Plasma oncotic pressure is capped at 25 mmHg
options.D: Plasma proteins remain trapped inside nuclear pores

questions.explanation: Large hydrophilic macromolecules require vesicular routes such as transcytosis rather than lipid diffusion.

questions.question: When a secretory gland cell is stimulated to dump stored hormone packets rapidly into ECF, the final membrane step is:

options.A: Pinocytosis of secreted hormone from interstitial space
options.B: Endosmosis shifting water into intracellular lysosomes
options.D: Exocytosis via secretory vesicle fusion with membrane

questions.explanation: Vesicle fusion discharges secretory cargo outward.

questions.question: An experimental inhibitor blocks carrier conformational cycling ONLY when two transported solutes travel in OPPOSITE directions; which mechanism halts while coupled inward Na+/glucose uptake persists:

options.A: Antiporter exchange such as Na+/H+ counter-transport, while symport persists
options.B: Symporter transport such as Na+/glucose co-transport, while antiport accelerates
options.C: Passive uncharged O2 diffusion across phospholipid tails
options.D: Clathrin-mediated receptor binding on apical membranes

questions.explanation: Antiporters exchange solutes in opposite directions, whereas symporters move co-transported solutes in the same direction.

questions.question: Why does a carrier that moves 2 solutes together in the SAME direction still qualify as active for one of them when ATP is NOT burned at that protein:

options.A: Both co-transported solutes move purely downhill
options.B: Downhill flux of one solute powers uphill co-transport
options.C: Hydrostatic filtration pushes solutes across lipids
options.D: Osmosis converts cytosolic glucose into sodium ions

questions.explanation: Coupled secondary active symport harvests electrochemical gradient energy.

questions.question: In renal or capillary barriers, hydrostatic filtration moves both water and suitable dissolved solutes together because:

options.A: Hydrostatic pressure carries Na+ while blocking water
options.B: Bulk filtration proceeds via receptor-mediated pits
options.C: Pressure-driven bulk flow moves water and filterable solutes
options.D: Hydrostatic filtration occurs only across nuclear pores

questions.explanation: Bulk flow moves fluid mass and filterable solutes collectively.

questions.question: Which factor alters the direction of net osmotic water flow across a selective cell membrane:

options.A: Reversing which side has higher effective solute level
options.C: Doubling phagocytic vacuole diameter inside neutrophils
options.D: Altering ATP while membranes stay impermeable

questions.explanation: Effective osmotic concentration gradient dictates endosmosis vs exosmosis.
