questions.question: If a toxin arrests ALL ATP-dependent active ion pumps across epithelial and excitable membranes (sparing simple gas diffusion), which set of solutes listed on Page 5 loses active pumping:

options.A: O2, CO2, and small lipid gases stop crossing the bilayer immediately
options.B: Macromolecular plasma albumin escapes via primary Cl- uniporters
options.C: Osmotic water molecules require direct Na+/K+-ATPase binding to cross pores
options.D: Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- gradients collapse while O2/CO2 continue diffusing passively

questions.explanation: Page 5 lists Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- among actively transported ions, whereas lipid-soluble gases cross passively.

questions.question: Why can gated channels act as cellular switches during signaling without burning ATP per passing ion:

options.A: Open channel pores synthesize ATP per ion cycle
options.B: Channel gating lets stored gradients drive passive flux
options.C: Chemical ligands bind clathrin to pull ions inward
options.D: Voltage gates actively pump ions uphill via ATP

questions.explanation: Opening a pre-charged electrochemical gradient allows rapid passive signaling.

questions.question: A cell displays rapid, saturable amino acid uptake when Na+ is high outside, which drops sharply when Na+/K+-ATPase is blocked. Best conclusion:

options.A: Amino acids diffuse passively across membrane lipids
options.B: Amino acids enter solely via macrophage phagocytosis
options.C: Amino acid uptake uses secondary Na+ co-transport
options.D: Amino acids filter solely via hydrostatic pressure

questions.explanation: Dependence on the Na+/K+-ATPase-maintained Na+ gradient identifies secondary Na+ symport.

questions.question: Which error appears in a student statement: 'Facilitated diffusion moves glucose uphill against its gradient because it uses a carrier protein':

options.A: Uncoupled carriers only facilitate downhill transport
options.B: Glucose diffuses straight through phospholipids unaided
options.C: Membrane carriers exclusively export waste gases
options.D: Glucose cannot cross membranes via protein carriers

questions.explanation: Carriers determine specificity and saturation, not uphill capability on their own.

questions.question: Compare pinocytosis with receptor-mediated endocytosis regarding selectivity and efficiency for scarce ligands:

options.A: Pinocytosis concentrates scarce hormones far more selectively
options.B: Receptors selectively concentrate scarce ligands in pits
options.C: Both processes require large phagocytic pseudopods
options.D: Neither process packages cargo inside vesicles

questions.explanation: Receptor binding adds targeted specificity over non-selective fluid sampling.

questions.question: If a toxin blocks fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane, which two processes fail directly:

options.A: Simple oxygen gas diffusion and osmotic endosmosis
options.B: Osmotic pressure and glomerular capillary filtration
options.C: Ligand channel gating and phospholipid dissolution
options.D: Secretory exocytosis and transcytosis exit step

questions.explanation: Both exocytosis and transcytosis conclude with vesicle-membrane fusion.

questions.question: Why does the chapter distinguish between 'no direct ATP' and 'uses a gradient created previously by pumps':

options.A: Secondary transport needs no direct ATP yet needs pump gradients
options.B: Primary active ATPases operate without spending ATP
options.C: Simple diffusion consumes stored Na+ ion gradients
options.D: Water osmosis requires clathrin-coated ATPase pits

questions.explanation: This clarifies the thermodynamic link between primary and secondary active transport.

questions.question: Which combination pairs transport mechanism with its true directional rule:

options.A: Primary active: against gradient using ATP directly
options.B: Passive simple diffusion: uphill using stored Na+ gradient
options.C: Secondary active: couples uphill flux to a downhill gradient

questions.explanation: Primary uses direct ATP uphill; secondary couples uphill movement to a downhill gradient.

questions.question: What happens to resting cytosolic [Na+] and membrane charge bias if Ca2+-ATPase works normally but Na+/K+-ATPase stops permanently:

options.A: Intracellular K+ rises steadily above normal limits
options.B: Cytosolic Na+ rises; +1 outward pump current ceases
options.C: Na+/glucose symport gains stronger inward driving force
options.D: Endosmosis stops because extracellular Cl- disappears

questions.explanation: Halting Na+/K+-ATPase lets Na+ accumulate and removes electrogenic Na+/K+ pumping.

questions.question: When intracellular acidity increases, cells extrude H+ uphill WITHOUT spending ATP directly at the transporter by coupling flux through:

options.A: Na+/glucose symport carrying both Na+ and H+ inward together
options.B: Uniporter carrier diffusion of glucose down concentration
options.C: Na+/H+ antiport linking downhill Na+ influx to opposite-direction H+ extrusion
options.D: Endosmotic water influx neutralizing cytosolic protons

questions.explanation: Counter-transport (Na+/H+ antiport) harnesses the inward Na+ gradient to expel H+ in the opposite direction.

questions.question: During phagocytic defense by a neutrophil, why must lysosomes fuse after phagosome closure rather than dumping enzymes freely into cytosol:

options.A: Neutrophils lack selective outer plasma membranes
options.B: Phagolysosome containment digests cargo, sparing host
options.C: Hydrolase lysosomes act only outside cells via exit
options.D: Clathrin coat cages directly digest bacterial walls

questions.explanation: Compartmentalized fusion protects host cytoplasm while digesting internalized microbes.

questions.question: If two compartments have identical effective solute concentrations across a semipermeable membrane, endosmosis and exosmosis cancel out with zero net osmotic water shift.
questions.explanation: Equal effective osmotic concentrations eliminate net osmotic water movement.

questions.question: Facilitated diffusion cannot become saturated even when every carrier binding site is continuously occupied.
questions.explanation: Finite binding sites and turnover rates produce saturation at high solute concentrations.

questions.question: Both Na+/glucose co-transport and Na+/Ca2+ counter-transport weaken when Na+/K+-ATPase is inhibited.
questions.explanation: Both rely on the inward Na+ gradient sustained by Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.question: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, clathrin itself acts as the cell-surface receptor that selects specific extracellular hormones.
questions.explanation: Specific membrane receptors recognize ligands; clathrin forms the pit coat protein.

questions.question: Transcytosis enables macromolecules to cross endothelial barriers without crossing passively through membrane lipid tails.
questions.explanation: Cargo moves inside vesicles via endocytosis on one pole and exocytosis on the opposite pole.

questions.question: Both hydrostatic filtration and osmotic water movement depend on direct ATP hydrolysis for every moving water molecule.
questions.explanation: Filtration is pressure-driven bulk movement and osmosis is passive solvent movement across a selective barrier.

questions.question: Ungated channels actively hydrolyze ATP to maintain a permanently open pore.
questions.explanation: Ungated channels require no ATP; flux through open pores remains passive.

questions.question: Primary active Ca2+-ATPases and secondary Na+/Ca2+ exchangers both work to move Ca2+ across membranes using cellular energy sources.
questions.explanation: Ca2+-ATPase spends ATP directly while Na+/Ca2+ exchange taps the Na+ gradient.

questions.question: Phagocytosis engulfs tiny dissolved droplets non-selectively without forming a phagosome.
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis takes in small fluid droplets; phagocytosis engulfs large particles inside a phagosome.

questions.question: Exocytosis releases vesicle contents outside the cell, whereas endocytosis internalizes extracellular fluid, ligands, or particles.
questions.explanation: Endocytosis imports cargo and exocytosis exports vesicular cargo.

questions.question: Which general transport group moves substances down a chemical or electrochemical gradient with NO direct ATP use:
questions.explanation: Passive processes proceed spontaneously down gradients without direct ATP expenditure.

questions.question: For ions, both concentration and electrical charge differences combine into the:
questions.explanation: Ion movement follows the combined chemical and electrical gradients.

questions.question: Which gaseous wastes and nutrients diffuse straight across phospholipid tails rather than waiting on vesicular endocytosis:
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic small gases dissolve directly across the bilayer.

questions.question: How do gated channels differ from ungated channels:

options.A: Gated channels change open state upon voltage or ligand stimulation
options.B: Gated channels require ATP for every ion

questions.explanation: Voltage or chemical ligands regulate gated channel opening.

questions.question: Why does facilitated diffusion saturate at high solute concentrations while simple diffusion does not:

options.A: ATP disappears only during simple diffusion
options.B: Glucose becomes hydrophobic at high levels
options.D: Carrier proteins have limited binding sites and turnover rates

questions.explanation: Finite carrier capacity caps maximal facilitated transport rate.

questions.question: Which change generally INCREASES passive diffusion rate across a cell membrane:

options.C: Higher temperature and steeper concentration gradient

questions.explanation: Stronger driving force and thermal energy accelerate diffusion.

questions.question: Movement of water and small dissolved solutes across glomerular capillaries driven by hydrostatic pressure is:
questions.explanation: Bulk filtration is driven by a hydrostatic pressure difference.

questions.question: Net osmotic entry of water INTO a cell is called:
questions.explanation: Water moving into cells down its osmotic gradient is endosmosis.

questions.question: Which term names osmotic pressure contributed specifically by blood plasma proteins (~25 mmHg):
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins exert colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure of roughly 25 mmHg.

questions.question: A membrane carrier handling only ONE specific solute species per transport cycle is classified as a:
questions.explanation: A single-solute carrier is a uniporter, rather than a symporter, antiporter, or pinocytic pit.

questions.question: Which pair matches transporter directionality accurately:

options.A: Symport = one solute; Uniport = opposite ways
options.B: Symport = same way; Antiport = opposite ways
options.C: Antiport = same way; Symport = bulk fluid
options.D: Uniport = vesicle export; Antiport = channel leak

questions.explanation: Co-transport moves solutes together; counter-transport exchanges them in opposite directions.

questions.question: What stoichiometry does the Na+/K+-ATPase execute per complete ATP cycle:
questions.explanation: Exporting 3 Na+ for 2 K+ sustains low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+.

questions.question: Because Na+/K+-ATPase transfers unequal positive ions per ATP cycle, the pump is:
questions.explanation: Unequal 3:2 cation pumping creates net electrogenic outward charge flow.

questions.question: Which primary pumps lower cytosolic calcium or secrete acid across selected membranes:
questions.explanation: Ca2+-ATPases and H+-ATPases actively pump Ca2+ and protons using ATP.

questions.question: Why is the Na+/glucose symporter NOT a primary ATP pump:

options.A: It couples uphill glucose entry to the downhill Na+ gradient created elsewhere
options.C: It pumps glucose out by exocytosis
options.D: It burns NADH inside the bilayer

questions.explanation: Secondary active symport relies on stored ion-gradient energy rather than direct ATP cleavage.

questions.question: Which pair represents sodium CO-TRANSPORT vs sodium COUNTER-TRANSPORT:

options.C: Na+/glucose = co-transport; Na+/Ca2+ and Na+/H+ = counter-transport

questions.explanation: Glucose moves with Na+, while Ca2+ and H+ exchange opposite to Na+.

questions.question: Cellular uptake of small droplets of extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes occurs via:
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis invaginates the plasma membrane to capture fluid-phase droplets.

questions.question: Which immune defense cells specialize in phagocytosis of bacteria and debris inside a phagosome:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf large particles into phagosomes for lysosomal digestion.

questions.question: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, what makes clathrin essential WITHOUT making it the receptor:

options.A: Clathrin hydrolyzes Na+ directly inside pores
options.B: Clathrin coats the vesicle pit after ligands bind
options.C: Clathrin circulates as an extracellular hormone

questions.explanation: Surface receptors select ligands; clathrin coats the invaginating pit.

questions.question: Which vesicular pathway transfers selected cargo from one surface of an endothelial cell to the opposite surface:
questions.explanation: Transcytosis combines endocytosis, cross-cell vesicle transit, and opposite-pole exocytosis.

questions.question: Fusion of an intracellular secretory vesicle with the plasma membrane to expel cargo outside is:
questions.explanation: Exocytosis releases cellular products to the extracellular environment.

questions.question: Which ion list contains the five ions highlighted under active transport in Chapter 3:
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies Na+, K+, Ca2+, H+, and Cl- among actively transported ions.

questions.question: When a cell takes up macromolecular cargo too large for channels/carriers, it uses:
questions.explanation: Vesicular transport handles cargo too bulky for channels or carriers.

questions.question: Which comparison cleanly distinguishes OSMOSIS from FILTRATION:

options.A: Osmosis requires ATPase; filtration requires clathrin pits
options.B: Osmosis moves plasma proteins; filtration moves nuclear DNA
options.C: Osmosis pulls water by solutes; filtration pushes fluid by pressure
options.D: Filtration occurs exclusively inside mitochondrial cristae

questions.explanation: Different driving forces distinguish osmotic vs hydrostatic transport.

questions.question: Simple diffusion directly through membrane lipids saturates quickly at moderate solute concentrations.
questions.explanation: Saturation occurs in carrier-mediated transport due to finite binding sites.

questions.question: Water exiting a cell down an osmotic gradient is called exosmosis.
questions.explanation: Endosmosis is osmotic water entry; exosmosis is osmotic water exit.

questions.question: Typical plasma oncotic pressure generated by colloidal blood proteins is approximately 25 mmHg.
questions.explanation: The reference specifies approximately 25 mmHg for plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure.

questions.question: A sodium-glucose symporter hydrolyzes ATP directly on its own protein subunits.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses this common exam trap: it relies secondarily on the Na+ gradient.

questions.question: Clathrin serves as the extracellular hormone-binding receptor rather than a vesicle coat protein.
questions.explanation: Specific membrane receptors bind ligands while clathrin forms the coating protein on the pit.

questions.question: Phagosomes fuse with lysosomal compartments to digest engulfed microorganisms and debris.
questions.explanation: Lysosomal fusion supplies hydrolytic enzymes to degrade phagocytosed cargo.
